title: The Truth About People Pleasing
author: Adam Grant
summary: Organizational psychologist Adam Grant reflects on his own history as a 'recovering people pleaser,' arguing that chronic accommodation of others is not really an act of kindness but a strategy for securing approval and avoiding rejection. Drawing on psychological research, he explains that people pleasing is rooted in insecure attachment and the fear of being disliked, meaning self-worth becomes contingent on how others react rather than on one's own values. Grant reframes the behavior as self-focused rather than selfish: the people pleaser avoids the discomfort of making others uncomfortable, which paradoxically can harm the very people they are trying to protect, such as the next passenger who inherits a too-cold Uber. He is careful to distinguish the origin of the behavior, often a genuine survival strategy learned in childhood, from its current function, arguing that the two should not be conflated. The piece closes with a reframing of boundary-setting as an act of self-respect rather than disrespect toward others.
points: Grant's central reframe: 'The root of chronic people pleasing is not concern for others. It's concern for their acceptance and approval.'
People pleasing is based on insecure attachment, learned when someone discovers others only value them when they are cooperative to the point of being submissive.
The behavior is self-focused, not selfish: avoiding a driver's discomfort about a cold car sets up the next passenger to shiver, meaning the accommodation doesn't even serve the intended beneficiary.
Grant distinguishes origin from current function: a fear-based survival strategy from the past does not need to remain the operating principle in the present.
His practical reframe: saying no is 'an act of self-preservation,' and sharing preferences is 'an expression of self-respect' rather than a display of disrespect.
quotes: The root of chronic people pleasing is not concern for others. It's concern for their acceptance and approval.

Psychologists find that what underlies people pleasing is the fear of being disliked and rejected. When we bend over backward to accommodate others at the expense of our own needs, it's because we depend on them for self-esteem.
Every time I failed to tell a driver that the car felt like Antarctica, I was setting another passenger up to shiver.
People pleasing is based on insecure attachment. We become people pleasers when we discover that others only value us when we're cooperative to the point of being submissive and deferential.
We shouldn't mistake the past origin of a behavior pattern for the current purpose it serves. A fear of being disliked leads too many of us to put our image above our values.
Sharing your preferences is not a display of disrespect. It's an expression of self-respect.
